discovery: Aberration correction in electron optics, enabling sub-ångström transmission and scanning transmission electron microscopy

nominees.name: Harald Rose
nominees.affiliation: Technische Universität Darmstadt / Ulm University, Germany

nominees.name: Ondrej L. Krivanek
nominees.affiliation: Nion Co., Kirkland, WA / Arizona State University, USA

subfield: Electron optics and condensed matter / materials physics
motivation: Scherzer showed in 1936 that round electron lenses cannot avoid spherical aberration, which for sixty years limited electron microscopes to resolutions far poorer than the electron wavelength permits. Harald Rose designed a practical hexapole corrector. Maximilian Haider built it and in 1998 demonstrated the first aberration-corrected TEM. Ondrej Krivanek independently built quadrupole-octupole correctors that made sub-ångström STEM and atom-by-atom spectroscopy possible. Their work changed what physicists can measure: single atoms, including light elements, can now be imaged, chemically identified and their bonding probed with EELS, and strain and polarisation can be mapped at the unit-cell level. Corrected instruments are now standard in laboratories worldwide. They underpin advances in quantum materials, oxide interfaces, catalysts, batteries, semiconductors and structural alloys. Few instrumental achievements have opened such a broad window onto matter, and this one meets Nobel's criterion of greatest benefit.
